SMT solving from R with z3r

Source: vignettes/z3r.Rmd
z3r.Rmd

z3r connects R to Z3, a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver. You describe a problem as logical constraints over integers, exact reals, Booleans, bit-vectors, arrays, strings and functions; Z3 either finds values that satisfy all of them, proves that none exist, or reports that it could not decide.

z3r is an independent third-party package. It is not developed or endorsed by Microsoft or by the Z3 team.

library(z3r)
z3_version()$runtime
#> [1] "5.4.1.0"

What an SMT solver does

An SMT solver answers one question: is there an assignment of values to these variables that makes all of these formulas true? The answer is

  • "sat": yes, and here is one (a model);
  • "unsat": no, provably not;
  • "unknown": Z3 gave up. This happens with resource limits, and with theories for which no complete algorithm exists (nonlinear integer arithmetic, quantifiers). "unknown" never means "unsat".

This differs from tools R users know:

Tool Works with Answers
optim(), nloptr continuous functions, floating point a local optimum, approximately
linear/integer programming (lpSolve, ompr) linear constraints a global optimum
computer algebra (SymPy, symcompR, Ryacas) symbolic expressions closed-form solutions, simplifications
SMT (Z3) arbitrary logical combinations of constraints in many theories a model, a proof of impossibility, or “unknown”

An SMT solver is the right tool when the problem is combinatorial or logical: disjunctions (“this job runs before that one, or after it”), implications, integer and bit-level reasoning, and questions of the form “does this hold for all inputs?”. Numbers are exact: integers have unbounded size and reals are rationals or algebraic numbers, never rounded floating point.

A first problem 

ctx <- z3_context()
x <- z3_int(ctx, "x")
y <- z3_int(ctx, "y")

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x + y == 10, x > 2 * y, y > 0)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "sat"
m <- z3_model(s)
m
#> <z3_model>
#>   y = 1
#>   x = 9
z3_value(z3_eval(m, x))
#> [1] 9

The three objects are always the same: a context owns everything, a solver collects constraints, and a model holds the values found by the last satisfiable check.

Constraints are built with ordinary R operators. They do not compute anything; they build formulas:

x + y == 10
#> <z3_expr Bool> (= (+ x y) 10)
x^2 + y^2 <= 25
#> <z3_expr Bool> (<= (+ (* x x) (* y y)) 25)

R’s && and || cannot be overloaded, so use &, |, ! or the functions z3_and(), z3_or(), z3_not(), z3_implies():

p <- z3_bool(ctx, "p")
z3_implies(p, x > 0) & (p | y < 0)
#> <z3_expr Bool> (and (=> p (> x 0)) (or p (< y 0)))

A formula is never silently converted to TRUE or FALSE, so mistakes such as if (x > 0) are errors rather than wrong answers:

if (x > 0) "positive"
#> Error in `if (x > 0) ...`:
#> ! argument is not interpretable as logical

Exact numbers

Z3 integers are unbounded and Z3 reals are exact, so z3r never passes values through double precision unless asked to:

big <- z3_int_val(ctx, "123456789012345678901234567890")
z3_simplify(big * big)
#> <z3_expr Int> 15241578753238836750495351562536198787501905199875019052100
z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3") + z3_real_val(ctx, "1/6")
#> <z3_expr Real> (+ (/ 1.0 3.0) (/ 1.0 6.0))
z3_simplify(z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3") + z3_real_val(ctx, "1/6"))
#> <z3_expr Real> (/ 1.0 2.0)

R numbers mixed with formulas are converted by a documented rule (see ?z3_int_val): whole numbers become exact integers, and 0.1 becomes the rational 1/10, which is the number R prints, not the binary approximation R stores. Whole numbers beyond 2^53 are refused, because R may already have rounded them; pass such numbers as strings or gmp::bigz.

Converting results back to R is exact as well. z3_value() returns a double only when the value is exactly representable, and otherwise a gmp number (or a string when gmp is not installed):

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
r <- z3_real(ctx, "r")
z3_add(s, x == z3_int_val(ctx, "1180591620717411303424"), 3 * r == 1)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "sat"
z3_model_values(z3_model(s))
#> $x
#> Big Integer ('bigz') :
#> [1] 1180591620717411303424
#> 
#> $r
#> Big Rational ('bigq') :
#> [1] 1/3

Division follows R: / is real division even for integers. %/% and %% are Z3’s integer div and mod, which use the SMT-LIB (Euclidean) convention. It agrees with R for positive divisors and differs for negative ones:

z3_simplify(z3_int_val(ctx, 7) %/% -2)
#> <z3_expr Int> (- 3)
7 %/% -2
#> [1] -4

Nonlinear problems and algebraic numbers

Z3 decides nonlinear real arithmetic exactly. Irrational solutions are algebraic numbers:

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, r * r == 2, r > 0)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "sat"
root <- z3_eval(z3_model(s), r)
root
#> <z3_expr Real> (root-obj (+ (^ x 2) (- 2)) 2)
z3_decimal(root, 20)
#> [1] "1.41421356237309504880?"
z3_value(root, exact = FALSE)
#> [1] 1.414214

Nonlinear integer arithmetic is undecidable in general, so Z3 may answer "unknown" or run for a long time. Limits keep checks bounded:

z <- z3_int(ctx, "z")
s <- z3_solver(ctx, timeout = 500)
z3_add(s, x > 0, y > 0, z > 0, x^3 + y^3 == z^3)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "unknown"
z3_reason_unknown(s)
#> [1] "timeout"

Use rlimit instead of timeout for results that are reproducible across machines. Ctrl-C also stops a running check.

Proving things for all inputs

To prove that a formula is always true, ask whether its negation can be satisfied. "unsat" is a proof.

a <- z3_int(ctx, "a")
b <- z3_int(ctx, "b")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, !(z3_abs(a + b) <= z3_abs(a) + z3_abs(b)))
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "unsat"

The triangle inequality holds for every pair of (unbounded) integers. No amount of random testing gives that guarantee.

A realistic example: scheduling with disjunctions

Three jobs share one machine. Each has a duration and a release time; job 2 must finish before job 3 starts. We want the earliest time at which all jobs are done. The “no overlap” requirement is a disjunction for every pair, so the feasible region is not convex, and gradient-based optimizers such as optim() have nothing to follow; integer programming needs big-M reformulations. For an SMT optimizer it is the natural formulation.

dur <- c(4, 3, 2)
release <- c(0, 1, 5)
start <- z3_ints(ctx, paste0("start", 1:3))

opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
for (i in 1:3) z3_add(opt, start[[i]] >= release[i])
for (i in 1:2) for (j in (i + 1):3) {
  z3_add(opt, start[[i]] + dur[i] <= start[[j]] | start[[j]] + dur[j] <= start[[i]])
}
z3_add(opt, start[[2]] + dur[2] <= start[[3]])
makespan <- z3_int(ctx, "makespan")
for (i in 1:3) z3_add(opt, makespan >= start[[i]] + dur[i])
obj <- z3_minimize(opt, makespan)

z3_check(opt)
#> [1] "sat"
z3_optimum(obj)
#> <z3_optimum> 9
unlist(z3_model_values(z3_model(opt))[paste0("start", 1:3)])
#> start1 start2 start3 
#>      0      4      7

The answer is optimal: Z3 proves no schedule finishes earlier.

Incremental solving

A solver keeps its assertions between checks. z3_push() and z3_pop() open and close scopes, which is how “what if” questions are asked without rebuilding the problem:

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x > 0, x < 10)
z3_push(s)
z3_add(s, x > 20)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "unsat"
z3_pop(s)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "sat"

Assumptions hold for a single check only:

z3_check(s, x == 5)
#> [1] "sat"
z3_check(s, x == 50)
#> [1] "unsat"

A model is only handed out for the check that produced it. After the solver changes, z3_model() refuses until the next z3_check(), so a model never describes constraints it was not computed for.

Explaining contradictions: unsatisfiable cores

Label constraints with z3_assert_and_track(). When the problem is unsatisfiable, z3_unsat_core() names a subset of the labels that is already contradictory:

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_assert_and_track(s, x > 10, "at_least_11")
z3_assert_and_track(s, x < 5, "at_most_4")
z3_assert_and_track(s, x != 7, "not_seven")
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "unsat"
names(z3_unsat_core(s))
#> [1] "at_least_11" "at_most_4"

Cores are not guaranteed to be minimal.

Optimization with soft constraints

Soft constraints are preferences with weights. The optimizer minimizes the total weight of the preferences it has to give up:

want <- z3_bools(ctx, c("coffee", "tea", "juice"))
opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
z3_add(opt, z3_or(!want$coffee, !want$tea))     # not both hot drinks
z3_add(opt, z3_or(!want$tea, !want$juice))
z3_add_soft(opt, want$coffee, 2)
z3_add_soft(opt, want$tea, 3)
z3_add_soft(opt, want$juice, 2)
z3_check(opt)
#> [1] "sat"
unlist(z3_model_values(z3_model(opt)))
#> coffee    tea  juice 
#>   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE

Optimal values are not always attained or finite; z3_optimum() reports "unbounded" and "not attained" (an infimum or supremum approached with an infinitesimal epsilon) instead of inventing a number:

opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
z3_add(opt, r < 3)
z3_optimum({
  h <- z3_maximize(opt, r)
  z3_check(opt)
  h
})
#> <z3_optimum> 3 (supremum, not attained)
